front: What is automatic storage duration in C++, when does an automatic object's destructor run, and how does it differ from dynamic storage duration? Predict the printed order for the code on the back before reading the output.
back:
Answer: An object with automatic storage duration (a local without new) lives from its declaration to the end of its enclosing block. Its destructor runs at that point, and locals are destroyed in reverse order of construction. An object created with new has dynamic storage duration: it lives until the matching delete, so the programmer controls the end of its life. The standard describes storage duration, not a stack; the stack is the usual implementation of automatic storage.

#include <cstdio>

struct Tracer {
    const char* name;
    explicit Tracer(const char* n) : name(n) { std::printf("ctor %s\n", name); }
    ~Tracer() { std::printf("dtor %s\n", name); }
};

int main() {
    Tracer outer{"outer"};
    {
        Tracer inner{"inner"};
        std::printf("in block\n");
    }                               // inner's automatic storage ends here
    std::printf("after block\n");
}
Output:
ctor outer
ctor inner
in block
dtor inner
after block
dtor outer
Used in the course for: every RAII class in modules 1-2 relies on this rule. Module 3 is about the cases where the end of life is not the end of a block.

Interview trap: returning the address of an automatic object, or a reference to a local, produces a dangling pointer. The compiler may warn, but the rule is the same whatever the optimisation level.

front: The expression new T(args) first calls {{c1::operator new}} to obtain raw storage, and then runs {{c2::the constructor}} on it. The expression delete p runs {{c3::the destructor}} and then calls {{c4::operator delete}} on the storage.
back:
Why it matters: allocation and construction are separate steps. This is why placement new, custom allocators (card 39) and std::make_unique are possible.

Interview trap: if the constructor throws inside new T(args), the runtime calls the matching operator delete on the storage. The expression then never yields a pointer, so there is nothing to leak in the caller.

front: A program allocates Blob* b = new Blob[3]; for a type with a user-declared destructor, and later calls delete b;. What is wrong? What does an unsanitized build print, and what does AddressSanitizer report?
back:
Answer: new[] must be paired with delete[]. Plain delete on the array pointer is undefined behaviour. For a type with a non-trivial destructor, the Itanium ABI makes new[] store a hidden element count before the array, and delete[] uses it to run every destructor. Plain delete frees the wrong address. GCC warns with -Wmismatched-new-delete, and the code is deliberately wrong below.

#include <cstdio>

struct Blob {
    int payload[4];
    ~Blob() { std::puts("~Blob"); }
};

int main() {
    Blob* b = new Blob[3];
    delete b;                       // BUG: should be delete[] b
    std::puts("done");
}
Output without sanitizers (exit code 134):Output:
free(): invalid pointer
AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address) report, first lines:
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed: 0x… in thread T0
    #0 0x… in operator delete(void*, unsigned long) ../../../../src/libsanitizer/asan/asan_new_delete.cpp:164
    #1 0x… in main src/m3_03.cpp:10
    #2 0x… in __libc_start_call_main ../sysdeps/nptl/libc_start_call_main.h:58
The reported region is 56 bytes: three 16-byte Blobs plus the 8-byte count. The pointer is 8 bytes inside it, which is why the free is rejected. The ~Blob message never prints.

Interview trap: the fix is delete[] b;, or better a std::vector<Blob> or std::unique_ptr<Blob[]>. Even with the right operator, a mismatched pair is UB, so the rule is the pairing, not the choice of pointer type.

front: A raw pointer keeps being used after delete, and a second delete is applied to the same address. Name the two bugs, say why the first can appear to work, and state what the code on the back prints without sanitizers and what AddressSanitizer reports.
back:
Answer: use-after-free is any access through a pointer after its object was deleted. The freed memory still holds the old bytes or has been reused, so the read may return the stale value by accident. Double free is a second delete of the same address; the allocator's free list is corrupted, and the failure may appear much later, far from the cause. Both are undefined behaviour.

Use-after-free.
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    int* p = new int(42);
    int* alias = p;
    delete p;
    std::printf("value after delete: %d\n", *alias);   // BUG: use-after-free
}
GCC warns with -Wuse-after-free. The unsanitized build printed an arbitrary value (it was not 42, and the number changes between runs). AddressSanitizer reports:
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x…
READ of size 4 at 0x… thread T0
    #0 0x… in main src/m3_04.cpp:7
    #1 0x… in __libc_start_call_main ../sysdeps/nptl/libc_start_call_main.h:58
Double free.
#include <cstdio>
__attribute__((noinline)) void release(int* q) { delete q; }
int main() {
    int* p = new int(42);
    release(p);
    std::puts("first release done");
    release(p);                       // BUG: double free
    std::puts("unreachable in practice");
}
Unsanitized output (exit code 134): free(): double free detected in tcache 2.

Interview trap: setting the pointer to nullptr after delete only protects the variable you cleared, not the aliases. The structural fix is single ownership, which is what std::unique_ptr enforces (cards 6-10).

front: Why are raw owning pointers (T* p = new T with a manual delete) discouraged in modern C++? Use the code on the back to explain the failure mode a code review would flag, and state the live-allocation count that the program prints.
back:
Answer: three problems. (1) Exception and early-return unsafety: any throw or return between new and delete leaks. (2) The type says nothing about ownership: a T* in a signature does not tell the caller whether to delete it, whether it may be null, or whether it outlives the call. (3) Ownership is easy to duplicate: copying the pointer invites a double delete. RAII (module 2) fixes all three by tying delete to a destructor, and unique_ptr makes the ownership explicit in the type.

The example below counts live allocations with a replaced operator new. The count is taken with a replaced operator new, so the leak is visible without a sanitizer.

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>

static int live = 0;
void* operator new(std::size_t n) { ++live; return std::malloc(n); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { --live; std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { --live; std::free(p); }

struct Session {
    Session() { std::puts("open"); }
    ~Session() { std::puts("close"); }
};

void process(bool fail) {
    Session* s = new Session();     // raw owner
    if (fail) throw std::runtime_error("bad input");   // delete is never reached
    delete s;
}

int main() {
    try {
        process(true);
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::printf("caught: %s\n", e.what());
    }
    std::printf("live allocations after catch=%d\n", live);   // 1: the Session leaked
    process(false);
    std::printf("live allocations after normal call=%d\n", live);
}
Output:
open
caught: bad input
live allocations after catch=1
open
close
live allocations after normal call=1
Interview trap: the same leak appears with an early return, a break or a continue, not only with exceptions. Every exit path needs the cleanup, which is the reason to let a destructor do it.

front: What is the ownership model of std::unique_ptr<T>, what does its destructor do, and how large is it compared with a raw pointer on a 64-bit platform? Check your answer against the code on the back.
back:
Answer: exclusive ownership. Exactly one unique_ptr owns the object at any time. Its destructor calls the deleter (by default delete) if the pointer is non-null. It is move-only. With the default deleter, which is an empty class, the empty-base optimisation means the object is the same size as a raw pointer.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

int main() {
    auto p = std::make_unique<int>(7);
    std::printf("*p = %d\n", *p);
    std::printf("sizeof(int*) = %zu\n", sizeof(int*));
    std::printf("sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int>) = %zu\n", sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int>));
}
Output:
*p = 7
sizeof(int*) = 8
sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int>) = 8
Interview trap: unique_ptr adds no run-time cost over a manual delete, but it is not an array type. unique_ptr<T> calls delete, not delete[]. For arrays use unique_ptr<T[]> or a std::vector.

front: Why is std::make_unique<T>(args) preferred to std::unique_ptr<T>(new T(args))? What exception-safety hazard did pre-C++17 evaluation order create in a call such as f(std::unique_ptr<W>(new W(1)), risky()), and what changed in C++17?
back:
Answer: make_unique has no raw new and does not repeat the type name. It performs the same single allocation.

The hazard: before C++17 the compiler could evaluate new W(1), then risky(), before constructing the unique_ptr. If risky() threw, the W leaked. C++17 forbids interleaving the evaluation of separate arguments, so this particular leak cannot happen in C++17 even with an explicit new. make_unique remains the idiom because it removes the raw new altogether.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Widget {
    int id;
    explicit Widget(int i) : id(i) {}
};

void consume(std::unique_ptr<Widget> w, int extra) {
    std::printf("consume id=%d extra=%d\n", w->id, extra);
}

int risky() { return 3; }

int main() {
    consume(std::make_unique<Widget>(1), risky());
    auto a = std::make_unique<Widget>(2);
    std::printf("a->id = %d\n", a->id);
}
Output:
consume id=1 extra=3
a->id = 2
Interview trap: make_unique cannot take a custom deleter. For that you must use the unique_ptr constructor directly, and then the raw new is back in the call (see card 10).

front: Why does auto b = a; fail to compile when a is a std::unique_ptr<int>? Quote the essential part of the compiler error, and write the correct version.
back:
Answer: unique_ptr has a deleted copy constructor and a deleted copy assignment, so no second owner can exist. The compiler error (g++ 13, excerpt):
src/m3_08err.cpp:4:14: error: use of deleted function ‘std::unique_ptr<_Tp, _Dp>::unique_ptr(const std::unique_ptr<_Tp, _Dp>&) [with _Tp = int; _Dp = std::default_delete<int>]’
The correct version transfers ownership, and a is left null:

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

int main() {
    auto a = std::make_unique<int>(5);
    // auto b = a;                  // ill-formed: unique_ptr copy constructor is deleted
    auto b = std::move(a);          // ownership transferred
    std::printf("b=%d, a is %s\n", *b, a ? "non-null" : "null");
}
Output:
b=5, a is null
Interview trap: passing a unique_ptr by value to a function needs std::move at the call site. Returning one from a function does not, because the return is an implicit move. Candidates often write std::move on the return, which can block elision.

front: Predict the output of this code. What state is the moved-from unique_ptr in, and in which order are the two Nodes destroyed at the end of main?
back:
Answer: the moved-from unique_ptr is null, and the move does not run any destructor. Assigning a new value to a null unique_ptr destroys nothing. At the end of main the objects are destroyed in reverse order of declaration: q (declared last) first.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Node {
    int v;
    explicit Node(int x) : v(x) { std::printf("ctor %d\n", v); }
    ~Node() { std::printf("dtor %d\n", v); }
};

int main() {
    auto p = std::make_unique<Node>(1);
    auto q = std::move(p);
    std::printf("p is %s\n", p ? "set" : "null");
    std::printf("q->v = %d\n", q->v);
    p = std::make_unique<Node>(2);      // old p was null: nothing destroyed
    std::printf("end of main\n");
}
Output:
ctor 1
p is null
q->v = 1
ctor 2
end of main
dtor 1
dtor 2
Interview trap: assigning to a unique_ptr that owns an object calls reset, which deletes the old object first. That is the desired behaviour, but it means the destructor can run inside an assignment statement.

front: A team wants a unique_ptr to own a buffer allocated with malloc and freed with free. What deleter type do you choose, and how does that choice change the size of the smart pointer? Check the sizes on the back.
back:
Answer: the deleter is the second template parameter, so it is part of the type. A stateless functor object costs nothing because of the empty-base optimisation. A function pointer must be stored, which doubles the size on a 64-bit platform. A captureless lambda converts to a function pointer; a capturing lambda makes the pointer larger and can be named only through decltype.

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>

struct FreeDeleter {
    void operator()(void* p) const noexcept {
        std::printf("FreeDeleter called\n");
        std::free(p);
    }
};

int main() {
    using Stateless = std::unique_ptr<int, FreeDeleter>;
    using FnPtr     = std::unique_ptr<int, void (*)(void*)>;
    std::printf("sizeof(stateless deleter)  = %zu\n", sizeof(Stateless));
    std::printf("sizeof(function pointer)   = %zu\n", sizeof(FnPtr));
    Stateless a(static_cast<int*>(std::malloc(sizeof(int))));
    *a = 9;
    std::printf("value %d\n", *a);
}
Output:
sizeof(stateless deleter)  = 8
sizeof(function pointer)   = 16
value 9
FreeDeleter called
Interview trap: the deleter is called with the stored pointer, so its parameter type must accept it. Here std::free takes void* and the pointer is int*, which converts implicitly. A mismatch is a compile error where the type is written, not at the call.

front: A std::shared_ptr holds two pointers: one to the {{c1::managed object}} and one to a {{c2::control block}}. The control block holds the {{c3::strong reference count}} and the weak count. The object is destroyed when the strong count reaches zero.
back:
Code and output:
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

int main() {
    std::shared_ptr<int> a = std::make_shared<int>(10);
    std::printf("count=%ld\n", a.use_count());
    {
        auto b = a;
        std::printf("count=%ld\n", a.use_count());
    }
    std::printf("count=%ld\n", a.use_count());
    std::printf("sizeof(shared_ptr<int>)=%zu\n", sizeof(a));
}
Output:
count=1
count=2
count=1
sizeof(shared_ptr<int>)=16
Interview trap: use_count() is a snapshot. In multithreaded code another thread can change the count right after you read it, so never branch on it for logic.

front: What does std::make_shared<T>(args) save compared with std::shared_ptr<T>(new T(args)), and what is its trade-off? Check the allocation counts on the back.
back:
Answer: make_shared places the object and the control block in one allocation. The explicit new version makes two. The count below replaces operator new to make the difference visible.

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <new>

static int allocs = 0;
void* operator new(std::size_t n) { ++allocs; return std::malloc(n); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { std::free(p); }

struct Payload { double x[4]; };

int main() {
    allocs = 0;
    auto a = std::make_shared<Payload>();
    std::printf("make_shared: allocations=%d\n", allocs);

    allocs = 0;
    std::shared_ptr<Payload> b(new Payload());
    std::printf("shared_ptr(new): allocations=%d\n", allocs);
    std::printf("use_count=%ld %ld\n", a.use_count(), b.use_count());
}
Output:
make_shared: allocations=1
shared_ptr(new): allocations=2
use_count=1 1
Trade-off: the single block is freed only when the weak count also reaches zero. A large object therefore keeps its memory alive while any weak_ptr exists, even after its destructor has run. The constructor also cannot be told a custom deleter through make_shared.

Interview trap: shared_ptr<T>(new T) allocates the control block separately, and two shared_ptrs built from the same raw pointer create two independent control blocks, each of which deletes the object. The raw pointer must be given to exactly one owner.

front: Each copy of a shared_ptr updates the reference count in the control block. What synchronisation does that involve, is it safe to copy and destroy shared_ptr copies from several threads, and does the same guarantee protect the object they point to?
back:
Answer: the strong and weak counts are updated with atomic read-modify-write operations. Copying or destroying different shared_ptr objects that share one control block from several threads is therefore safe, and the final count is correct. The object itself gets no protection: concurrent access to it is a data race if any thread writes. A shared_ptr<T> does not make T const, so std::shared_ptr<const T> is the type that expresses read-only sharing.

The cost: an atomic increment and decrement, even uncontended, is tens of cycles (approximate, and it varies by CPU), and a cache line written by several cores bounces between them. A shared_ptr passed by value in a hot loop therefore costs real time. The count below is correct after four threads copy in a loop.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    auto data = std::make_shared<const std::vector<double>>(1000, 1.0);
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t) {
        ts.emplace_back([&data] {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) {
                auto local = data;          // atomic increment, then atomic decrement
            }
        });
    }
    for (auto& th : ts) th.join();
    std::printf("use_count after join=%ld\n", data.use_count());
}
Output:
use_count after join=1
Interview trap: const std::shared_ptr<T> makes the pointer const, not the object. Prefer const std::shared_ptr<T>& for a function that only uses the object, and pass T& if it does not need sharing at all.

front: Predict the output. Why is no destructor message printed, and what is the standard fix for the structure in this code?
back:
Answer: the parent and child each hold the other through a shared_ptr. Each count drops from 2 to 1 when a local goes out of scope, and never reaches 0, so neither object is destroyed. The destructors never run, and the memory is leaked.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Node {
    const char* name;
    std::shared_ptr<Node> parent;     // strong back-pointer: the bug
    std::shared_ptr<Node> child;
    explicit Node(const char* n) : name(n) {}
    ~Node() { std::printf("dtor %s\n", name); }
};

int main() {
    auto p = std::make_shared<Node>("parent");
    auto c = std::make_shared<Node>("child");
    p->child = c;
    c->parent = p;                    // strong cycle
    std::printf("use_count p=%ld c=%ld\n", p.use_count(), c.use_count());
}
Output:
use_count p=2 c=2
Standard fix: make the back-pointer a weak_ptr (card 15).

Interview trap: a cycle through unique_ptr cannot form, because each object has one owner. Cycles are a shared_ptr problem, and they are invisible to the compiler: the code compiles and runs cleanly.

front: The parent owns the child through a shared_ptr, and the child holds a non-owning back-pointer. What type should the back-pointer be, how do you use it safely, and what is the destruction order in the code on the back?
back:
Answer: std::weak_ptr. It observes the object without contributing to the strong count. lock() returns a shared_ptr that is non-null only if the object is still alive; expired() only reports the state, so always use lock() and check the result.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Node {
    const char* name;
    std::weak_ptr<Node> parent;       // non-owning back-pointer
    std::shared_ptr<Node> child;
    explicit Node(const char* n) : name(n) {}
    ~Node() { std::printf("dtor %s\n", name); }
};

int main() {
    auto p = std::make_shared<Node>("parent");
    {
        auto c = std::make_shared<Node>("child");
        p->child = c;
        c->parent = p;
        if (auto up = c->parent.lock()) std::printf("child sees %s\n", up->name);
    }
    std::printf("p.use_count=%ld\n", p.use_count());
    std::weak_ptr<Node> w = p;
    p.reset();
    std::printf("expired=%d\n", static_cast<int>(w.expired()));
    std::printf("lock is null=%d\n", w.lock() == nullptr);
}
Output:
child sees parent
p.use_count=1
dtor parent
dtor child
expired=1
lock is null=1
When the parent's last strong reference is reset, its destructor runs first, and destroying its child member then destroys the child. The weak_ptr held by main reports expired afterwards.

Interview trap: testing expired() and then calling lock() is a race in multithreaded code, because another thread can release the last owner in between. Call lock() once and test the returned pointer.

front: What is the aliasing constructor of std::shared_ptr, what does the resulting pointer keep alive, and when would a desk library use it? Predict the output on the back before reading it.
back:
Answer: std::shared_ptr<U>(owner, ptr) shares ownership of the control block of owner, but its get() returns ptr, which can point to any object, typically a sub-object of the owner. The owner stays alive as long as this pointer exists. Use it to hand out a pointer to a member, such as a column or a field of a trade record, without giving up the parent's lifetime.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Engine {
    int hp = 300;
    ~Engine() { std::puts("~Engine"); }
};
struct Car {
    Engine engine;
    ~Car() { std::puts("~Car"); }
};

int main() {
    std::shared_ptr<int> hp_ptr;
    {
        auto car = std::make_shared<Car>();
        hp_ptr = std::shared_ptr<int>(car, &car->engine.hp);   // aliasing constructor
        std::printf("hp=%d use_count=%ld\n", *hp_ptr, car.use_count());
    }
    std::printf("hp still=%d\n", *hp_ptr);
}
Output:
hp=300 use_count=2
hp still=300
~Car
~Engine
Interview trap: use_count() on the aliased pointer counts the owner's references, not the sub-object's. The aliased pointer must never be deleted separately: it was never allocated on its own, and the owner's destructor is the only one that runs.

front: Why does calling shared_from_this() inside a constructor throw std::bad_weak_ptr? When does it work, and what goes wrong if you create a second shared_ptr from this instead?
back:
Answer: enable_shared_from_this stores a weak_ptr in the base class, and that weak_ptr is bound when the first shared_ptr takes ownership. Inside a constructor no owner exists yet, so the call throws (since C++17). An object on the stack has no owner, so the call throws as well.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Task : std::enable_shared_from_this<Task> {
    Task() {
        try {
            auto self = shared_from_this();   // no owner exists yet
            (void)self;
        } catch (const std::bad_weak_ptr&) {
            std::puts("bad_weak_ptr in ctor");
        }
    }
    std::shared_ptr<Task> handle() { return shared_from_this(); }
};

int main() {
    auto owned = std::make_shared<Task>();
    auto h = owned->handle();
    std::printf("use_count=%ld\n", owned.use_count());
    Task on_stack;
    try {
        on_stack.handle();
    } catch (const std::bad_weak_ptr&) {
        std::puts("stack object: bad_weak_ptr");
    }
}
Output:
bad_weak_ptr in ctor
use_count=2
bad_weak_ptr in ctor
stack object: bad_weak_ptr
Interview trap: std::shared_ptr<Task>(this) creates a new, independent control block. Two control blocks mean two strong counts, so the object is deleted twice. This is the bug that enable_shared_from_this exists to prevent. The usual pattern is a factory that creates the shared_ptr and then calls a separate initialisation method.

front: Herb Sutter's guidance for function parameters: when should a function take T*, T&, const std::shared_ptr<T>&, std::shared_ptr<T> by value, or std::unique_ptr<T> by value? Give the rule for each.
back:
Answer:
  • T& (or const T&): the function uses the object and does not affect its lifetime. It cannot receive null.
  • T*: the same, but the argument may be null. It is a non-owning observer, not an owner.
  • const std::shared_ptr<T>&: the function may store or share ownership, but only if it needs to. No count change is made for the call.
  • std::shared_ptr<T> by value: the function will keep a copy, so the copy is made at the call site.
  • std::unique_ptr<T> by value: the function takes ownership. The caller must write std::move.
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Widget { int id; };

void use_only(const Widget& w)           { std::printf("use_only %d\n", w.id); }
void observe(Widget* w)                  { if (w) std::printf("observe %d\n", w->id); }
void store(std::shared_ptr<Widget> w)    { std::printf("store, count inside=%ld\n", w.use_count()); }
void sink(std::unique_ptr<Widget> w)     { std::printf("sink %d\n", w->id); }

int main() {
    auto sp = std::make_shared<Widget>(Widget{1});
    auto up = std::make_unique<Widget>(Widget{2});
    use_only(*sp);
    observe(sp.get());
    store(sp);                          // copies: count goes up for the call
    sink(std::move(up));                // ownership transferred
    std::printf("count after calls=%ld\n", sp.use_count());
}
Output:
use_only 1
observe 1
store, count inside=2
sink 2
count after calls=1
Interview trap: taking std::shared_ptr<T> by value only to read the object costs an atomic increment and decrement on every call, and it hides the fact that the function does not keep the object. Take T& instead.

front: A function that will keep ownership of a unique_ptr argument takes it by {{c1::value}}, and the caller must pass it with {{c2::std::move}}. A function that only uses the object should take it as {{c3::T&}} (or const T&) instead.
back:
Why: the by-value parameter is the only signature that can take ownership, because a unique_ptr cannot be copied. A reference signature says the function does not change the lifetime, which is the information a reader needs.

Interview trap: a const std::unique_ptr<T>& parameter is almost always wrong. It lets the function read and reset the pointer, but it cannot take ownership, so the caller's intent is unclear.

front: Every expression has a value category. A prvalue such as f() returning int is a {{c1::prvalue}}; std::move(x) is an {{c2::xvalue}}; the string literal "abc" is an {{c3::lvalue}}; and a named variable of type int&& is an {{c4::lvalue}}.
back:
Structure: a glvalue is an lvalue or an xvalue, and it has an identity you can take the address of. An rvalue is a prvalue or an xvalue, and it may be moved from. A name is an lvalue whatever its declared type.

Interview trap: decltype(x) gives the declared type of the name, but decltype((x)) with extra parentheses gives an lvalue reference, because the expression (x) is an lvalue.

front: Predict the output. Why does f(r) call the lvalue overload even though r is declared as int&&?
back:
Answer: a named rvalue reference is an lvalue expression. Inside f or in any expression, r has an address and can be used again, so overload resolution treats it as an lvalue. To pass it on as an rvalue you must cast it back with std::move, or forward it.

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

void f(int& x)  { std::printf("lvalue overload: %d\n", x); }
void f(int&& x) { std::printf("rvalue overload: %d\n", x); }

int main() {
    f(5);
    int a = 1;
    f(a);
    int&& r = 7;        // r is a named rvalue reference
    f(r);               // r is an lvalue expression
    f(std::move(r));
}
Output:
rvalue overload: 5
lvalue overload: 1
lvalue overload: 7
rvalue overload: 7
Interview trap: this is why a move constructor that writes data_(other.data_) leaves two owners of the same memory, and why a constructor that moves a member must write std::move(other.member) for every member that owns resources.

front: What does std::move do at run time, and where does the move actually take place? Check the claim on the code in the back.
back:
Answer: std::move(x) is a cast to T&&. It is implemented as static_cast<remove_reference_t<T>&&>(x) and generates no code of its own. The move happens in whichever constructor or assignment operator the resulting rvalue selects. Calling std::move and discarding the result does nothing.

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

int main() {
    int x = 3;
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(std::move(x)), int&&>);
    std::string s = "hello";
    std::string t = std::move(s);     // the move constructor runs here, not inside std::move
    std::printf("t=%s s.size=%zu\n", t.c_str(), s.size());
    auto&& r = std::move(t);          // a cast only: t is not touched
    std::printf("r.size=%zu t=%s\n", r.size(), t.c_str());
}
Output:
t=hello s.size=0
r.size=5 t=hello
Interview trap: std::move on a const object yields const T&&, which cannot bind to a move constructor. The copy constructor is selected instead, so the move silently becomes a copy.

front: After std::string t = std::move(s);, what state is s in, what may you do with it, and what does libstdc++ actually leave behind? Check the output on the back.
back:
Answer: the moved-from object is in a valid but unspecified state. The class invariants hold, so it can be destroyed and assigned to. Operations without preconditions (such as size() or clear()) are also allowed. Reading its value is not, because the value is unspecified.

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::string s(100, 'x');
    std::string t = std::move(s);
    std::printf("t.size=%zu s.size=%zu\n", t.size(), s.size());
    s = "reused";                     // assignment to a moved-from object is fine
    std::printf("s=%s\n", s.c_str());

    std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};
    std::vector<int> w = std::move(v);
    std::printf("v.size=%zu w.size=%zu\n", v.size(), w.size());
}
Output:
t.size=100 s.size=0
s=reused
v.size=0 w.size=3
The output shows what libstdc++ does in practice: the string and vector end up empty. That is an implementation choice, and code must not depend on it.

Interview trap: std::unique_ptr is the exception: its moved-from state is specified as null. Do not generalise that guarantee to other types.

front: Implement the move constructor and move assignment for a Buffer class that owns an int* and a size. What must move assignment do that the move constructor does not, and why should both be noexcept? The full class with its copy operations is on the back.
back:
Answer: the move constructor steals the pointer and nulls the source, so the source's destructor deletes nothing. Move assignment has an existing resource to release first, so it must call delete[] on its own pointer before taking the other one. It must also be safe when the operand is *this. Both are noexcept because they do not allocate, and that matters for std::vector (card 26).

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

class Buffer {
public:
    explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : data_(new int[n]{}), size_(n) {}
    ~Buffer() { delete[] data_; }

    Buffer(const Buffer& other) : data_(new int[other.size_]), size_(other.size_) {
        std::copy(other.data_, other.data_ + size_, data_);
    }
    Buffer& operator=(const Buffer& other) {
        if (this != &other) {
            Buffer tmp(other);
            swap(tmp);
        }
        return *this;
    }

    Buffer(Buffer&& other) noexcept
        : data_(std::exchange(other.data_, nullptr)),
          size_(std::exchange(other.size_, 0)) {}

    Buffer& operator=(Buffer&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            delete[] data_;                            // release our old resource first
            data_ = std::exchange(other.data_, nullptr);
            size_ = std::exchange(other.size_, 0);
        }
        return *this;
    }

    void swap(Buffer& o) noexcept {
        std::swap(data_, o.data_);
        std::swap(size_, o.size_);
    }
    std::size_t size() const noexcept { return size_; }

private:
    int* data_;
    std::size_t size_;
};

int main() {
    Buffer a(4);
    Buffer b = std::move(a);
    std::printf("b.size=%zu a.size=%zu\n", b.size(), a.size());
    Buffer c(2);
    c = std::move(b);
    std::printf("c.size=%zu b.size=%zu\n", c.size(), b.size());
}
Output:
b.size=4 a.size=0
c.size=4 b.size=0
Interview trap: the copy-and-swap assignment handles self-assignment without an explicit check, at the cost of one extra move. Hand-written move assignment needs the check, as card 25 shows.

front: A class has a move assignment that deletes its pointer, takes the operand's pointer and nulls the operand. What happens under self move-assignment, x = std::move(x);? Predict the output on the back before reading it.
back:
Answer: the operator deletes p, copies the same pointer from the operand (which is itself), and then nulls it. The operand and the target are the same object, so the value is destroyed and the object is left holding nullptr. Nothing crashes, which is why the bug survives review. For a type whose members are more complicated, the same code leaves dangling state behind.

#include <cstdio>

struct Naive {
    int* p;
    explicit Naive(int v) : p(new int(v)) {}
    Naive& operator=(Naive&& o) {          // no self-assignment check
        delete p;
        p = o.p;
        o.p = nullptr;
        return *this;
    }
    ~Naive() { delete p; }
};

int main() {
    Naive x(42);
    Naive& alias = x;
    x = static_cast<Naive&&>(alias);       // self move-assignment
    std::printf("after self-move, p is %s\n", x.p ? "valid" : "null (value lost)");
}
Output:
after self-move, p is null (value lost)
Fix: test this != &other before releasing anything, as in card 24, or use copy-and-swap.

Interview trap: GCC warns on the literal form x = std::move(x); under -Wall (-Wself-move), so an interviewer may write the aliasing form instead, as in the snippet.

front: Why does std::vector copy rather than move its elements during reallocation when the element's move constructor is not noexcept? Predict the output of the two runs on the back.
back:
Answer: std::vector must keep the strong exception guarantee when it reallocates. If a move throws part way through, the old elements are already partly moved and cannot be restored. It therefore uses std::move_if_noexcept, which yields an rvalue only when the move constructor is noexcept or when the type has no usable copy constructor.

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct Loud {
    Loud() = default;
    Loud(const Loud&) { std::puts("  copy"); }
    Loud(Loud&&) noexcept { std::puts("  move"); }
};

struct Quiet {
    Quiet() = default;
    Quiet(const Quiet&) { std::puts("  copy"); }
    Quiet(Quiet&&) { std::puts("  move (not noexcept)"); }
};

template <class T>
void grow() {
    std::vector<T> v;
    v.reserve(1);
    v.emplace_back();
    std::puts("  -- second emplace_back forces reallocation");
    v.emplace_back();
}

int main() {
    std::puts("Loud:");  grow<Loud>();
    std::puts("Quiet:"); grow<Quiet>();
}
Output:
Loud:
  -- second emplace_back forces reallocation
  move
Quiet:
  -- second emplace_back forces reallocation
  copy
Interview trap: a move-only type, such as one holding a unique_ptr, is moved during reallocation whether or not its move constructor is noexcept, because there is no copy to fall back to. reserve avoids the reallocation altogether.

front: Mark move operations {{c1::noexcept}}. During reallocation std::vector uses {{c2::std::move_if_noexcept}}, which selects the move only if the move constructor is noexcept or the type is {{c3::not copy-constructible}}.
back:
Mechanism: move_if_noexcept returns const T& when the move may throw and a copy is available, so the copy constructor is selected. Standard-library types such as std::string and std::vector have noexcept move constructors, so they move during reallocation.

Interview trap: a noexcept move that actually throws calls std::terminate. Only mark a move noexcept if it cannot throw.

front: Since C++17, what does returning a prvalue such as return Big{}; cost in copies or moves? Is it still acceptable to return an 8 KB object by value? Predict the output of the code on the back.
back:
Answer: nothing. A prvalue does not create a temporary that is then moved; the object is initialised directly in the caller's storage. This is guaranteed copy elision, so the copy and move constructors need not even exist. Returning an 8 KB object by value is therefore fine, and it is clearer than an output parameter.

#include <array>
#include <cstdio>

struct Big {
    std::array<double, 1000> data{};
    Big() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    Big(const Big&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    Big(Big&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
};

Big make() { return Big{}; }          // returns a prvalue: no copy or move since C++17

int main() {
    Big b = make();
    std::printf("size=%zu\n", b.data.size());
}
Output:
ctor
size=1000
Interview trap: the guarantee covers prvalues only. A named local is covered by NRVO, which is optional (card 29).

front: What is NRVO, is it guaranteed, and what happens when a function returns one of two different named locals? Predict the output on the back, then explain it.
back:
Answer: named return value optimisation constructs a single named local directly in the caller's return slot. The standard allows it but does not require it. With one named object returned on every path, compilers usually apply it. With two different named objects the compiler cannot choose one storage location, so it falls back to an implicit move of the returned local.

#include <cstdio>

struct Obj {
    Obj() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    Obj(const Obj&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    Obj(Obj&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
};

Obj single_named() { Obj o; return o; }            // NRVO candidate: one named object

Obj two_named(bool c) {
    Obj a;
    Obj b;
    if (c) return a;
    return b;                                       // NRVO not applicable: fallback to implicit move
}

int main() {
    std::puts("single_named:");
    Obj x = single_named();
    std::puts("two_named:");
    Obj y = two_named(true);
    (void)x; (void)y;
}
Output:
single_named:
ctor
two_named:
ctor
ctor
move
Interview trap: return std::move(o); on a single local blocks the implicit move as well as NRVO. GCC warns with -Wpessimizing-move under -Wall. Just write return o;.

front: In template<class T> void f(T&& x), why is T&& not always an rvalue reference? State what T deduces to for an lvalue, a prvalue and an xvalue argument, and check it on the back.
back:
Answer: T&& is a forwarding reference only when T is deduced in that exact form. An lvalue of type X deduces T = X&, and reference collapsing turns T&& into X&. A prvalue or an xvalue deduces T = X, which gives X&&. The rule uses reference collapsing: && collapses to & when either side is an lvalue reference.

#include <cstdio>
#include <type_traits>

template <class T>
void report(T&& x) {
    using U = decltype(x);
    std::printf("T is lvalue ref=%d, decltype(x) is lvalue ref=%d\n",
                static_cast<int>(std::is_lvalue_reference_v<T>),
                static_cast<int>(std::is_lvalue_reference_v<U>));
}

struct Cfg { int v; };

int main() {
    Cfg c{1};
    const Cfg k{3};
    report(c);                  // T = Cfg&
    report(Cfg{2});             // T = Cfg
    report(static_cast<Cfg&&>(c));   // T = Cfg
    report(k);                  // T = const Cfg&
}
Output:
T is lvalue ref=1, decltype(x) is lvalue ref=1
T is lvalue ref=0, decltype(x) is lvalue ref=0
T is lvalue ref=0, decltype(x) is lvalue ref=0
T is lvalue ref=1, decltype(x) is lvalue ref=1
Interview trap: std::vector<T>&& is a plain rvalue reference, because the deduced type is not a bare T. auto&& in a range-based for is a forwarding reference.

front: Why does a generic factory need std::forward<Args>(args)... rather than std::move or the bare names? Predict which overloads run for the two calls on the back.
back:
Answer: std::forward<T>(x) casts x to T&& only when T is a non-reference type. For an lvalue argument (T = X&) it yields an lvalue, and for an rvalue it yields an rvalue. So the category the caller supplied is preserved. std::move always yields an rvalue, which would silently move an lvalue the caller still owns.

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

struct Order {
    std::string sym;
    Order(const std::string& s) { std::puts("copy-construct from const&"); sym = s; }
    Order(std::string&& s)      { std::puts("move-construct from &&");     sym = std::move(s); }
};

template <class... Args>
Order make_order(Args&&... args) {
    return Order(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
}

int main() {
    std::string s = "ESTR";
    Order a = make_order(s);                     // lvalue argument
    Order b = make_order(std::string("EUR"));    // rvalue argument
    std::printf("%s %s\n", a.sym.c_str(), b.sym.c_str());
}
Output:
copy-construct from const&
move-construct from &&
ESTR EUR
Interview trap: after std::forward passes an rvalue on, the source object may be moved from. Do not use a forwarded argument again in the same function.

front: Predict the output. Why does bad() call the wrong overload of sink, even though its argument is an rvalue at the call site?
back:
Answer: inside bad, the parameter x has a name, so the expression x is an lvalue, whatever the category of the argument. sink(x) therefore selects the const std::string& overload. good() keeps the category with std::forward.

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

void sink(std::string&& s)      { std::printf("sink &&: %zu\n", s.size()); }
void sink(const std::string& s) { std::printf("sink const&: %zu\n", s.size()); }

template <class T> void bad(T&& x)  { sink(x); }                    // x is an lvalue here
template <class T> void good(T&& x) { sink(std::forward<T>(x)); }

int main() {
    bad(std::string("abc"));
    good(std::string("abc"));
}
Output:
sink const&: 3
sink &&: 3
Interview trap: this is a silent performance bug, not a compile error: the copy is correct, only slower. The same happens when a forwarding function passes one parameter to two callees. Forward it only at its last use.

front: What is the difference between push_back(Pt{1, 2}) and emplace_back(1, 2), and when does the difference disappear? Predict the output on the back.
back:
Answer: push_back receives an already-constructed element, so it constructs a temporary and then moves it into the vector. emplace_back forwards its arguments to the element's constructor and constructs the element in place. No temporary, so no move.

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct Pt {
    int x, y;
    Pt(int a, int b) : x(a), y(b) { std::puts("  ctor"); }
    Pt(const Pt&) { std::puts("  copy"); }
    Pt(Pt&&) noexcept { std::puts("  move"); }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Pt> v;
    v.reserve(4);
    std::puts("push_back(Pt{1, 2}):");
    v.push_back(Pt{1, 2});
    std::puts("emplace_back(1, 2):");
    v.emplace_back(1, 2);
    std::printf("size=%zu\n", v.size());
}
Output:
push_back(Pt{1, 2}):
  ctor
  move
emplace_back(1, 2):
  ctor
size=2
Interview trap: when you already hold an object, push_back(p) and emplace_back(p) both copy. The gain exists only when the element is built from arguments. Also, emplace_back(1, 2) can call an explicit constructor directly, while push_back({1, 2}) cannot, because the braced form needs an implicit conversion.

front: For struct Bad { char a; double b; char c; };, what are sizeof, alignof and the member offsets on x86-64 Linux? How do you reduce the size without changing the members? Check the numbers on the back.
back:
Answer: a double must be 8-byte aligned, so the compiler places padding after a. The struct's size is always a multiple of its alignment, so trailing padding is added after c. Ordering the members by decreasing alignment removes the internal padding.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>

struct Bad  { char a; double b; char c; };
struct Good { double b; char a; char c; };

int main() {
    std::printf("Bad:  sizeof=%zu alignof=%zu offsets a=%zu b=%zu c=%zu\n",
                sizeof(Bad), alignof(Bad), offsetof(Bad, a), offsetof(Bad, b), offsetof(Bad, c));
    std::printf("Good: sizeof=%zu alignof=%zu offsets b=%zu a=%zu c=%zu\n",
                sizeof(Good), alignof(Good), offsetof(Good, b), offsetof(Good, a), offsetof(Good, c));
    std::printf("alignof(double)=%zu\n", alignof(double));
}
Output:
Bad:  sizeof=24 alignof=8 offsets a=0 b=8 c=16
Good: sizeof=16 alignof=8 offsets b=0 a=8 c=9
alignof(double)=8
Interview trap: #pragma pack removes the padding, but it produces misaligned members, which are slower and can fault on some architectures. Reordering is the portable fix.

front: On x86-64 Linux, struct { double b; char a; char c; } has sizeof {{c1::16}}: its members occupy 10 bytes, which is rounded up to a multiple of its alignment, {{c2::8}}.
back:
Rule: sizeof(T) is always a multiple of alignof(T). This keeps every element of an array of T aligned.

Interview trap: an empty class still has size 1, because distinct objects must have distinct addresses. An empty base class is the exception that the optimisation exploits (card 10).

front: Why can short std::strings avoid heap allocation, and at what length does libstdc++ start to allocate? Use the snippet on the back to check, and say what the threshold depends on.
back:
Answer: the string object contains an inline buffer (small-string optimisation). Short strings are stored inside the object, so creating one needs no allocation. In libstdc++ (GCC 13) sizeof(std::string) is 32 bytes and the inline capacity is 15 characters plus the terminator; 16 characters go to the heap.

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <new>
#include <string>

static int allocs = 0;
void* operator new(std::size_t n) { ++allocs; return std::malloc(n); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { std::free(p); }

int main() {
    std::printf("sizeof(std::string)=%zu\n", sizeof(std::string));
    allocs = 0;
    std::string shortS(15, 'a');
    std::printf("15 chars: heap allocations=%d, capacity=%zu\n", allocs, shortS.capacity());
    allocs = 0;
    std::string longS(16, 'a');
    std::printf("16 chars: heap allocations=%d, size=%zu\n", allocs, longS.size());
}
Output:
sizeof(std::string)=32
15 chars: heap allocations=0, capacity=15
16 chars: heap allocations=1, size=16
Interview trap: the threshold is implementation-specific: libc++ uses a different inline capacity, so never hard-code 15. Also, data() of a short string points into the object itself, so a move or copy changes the address. Pointers and string_views into a short string do not survive the move.

front: A function returns a std::span<const double> over a local std::vector. What is wrong, what does an unsanitized build print, and what does AddressSanitizer report? Check the code on the back.
back:
Answer: std::span is a non-owning view of a contiguous range. The vector owns the buffer, and the buffer is freed when the function returns, so the span dangles. The compiler did not warn about it (g++ 13, -Wall -Wextra).

#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <vector>

std::span<const double> curve_pillars() {
    std::vector<double> pillars{0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0};
    return pillars;                 // BUG: span views the vector's buffer, which dies here
}

int main() {
    std::span<const double> s = curve_pillars();
    std::printf("first pillar=%f\n", s[0]);
}
Unsanitized output (the read happened to return zero):Output:
first pillar=0.000000
AddressSanitizer report, first lines:
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x…
READ of size 8 at 0x… thread T0
    #0 0x… in main src/m3_37.cpp:12
    #1 0x… in __libc_start_call_main ../sysdeps/nptl/libc_start_call_main.h:58
Fix: return the std::vector<double> by value and let the caller own it, then take a span from the caller's object.

Interview trap: a span returned from a function is safe only when it views storage that outlives the function, such as a member, a static, or the caller's data.

front: Why is std::string_view sv = std::string(...) + ...; a bug? Name the extra property of string_view that makes passing sv.data() to a C API unsafe, and check the sanitizer output on the back.
back:
Answer: the temporary std::string is destroyed at the end of the full declaration, which leaves name viewing freed memory. The string is longer than 15 characters, so it is on the heap, and AddressSanitizer reports the use-after-free. The compiler did not warn.

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

int main() {
    std::string_view name = std::string("EUR_SOFR_ESTR_20260101");   // BUG: temporary dies at ';'
    std::printf("size=%zu first char=%c\n", name.size(), name[0]);   // read is instrumented
}
AddressSanitizer report, first lines:
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x…
READ of size 1 at 0x… thread T0
    #0 0x… in main src/m3_38.cpp:7
    #1 0x… in __libc_start_call_main ../sysdeps/nptl/libc_start_call_main.h:58
Interview trap: a string_view is not null-terminated. Passing sv.data() to a function that reads until a zero byte reads past the end of the view. Use std::string when a C API needs a terminator.

front: A Monte Carlo pricer allocates scratch storage for every path. Sketch the arena (bump) allocator that removes those allocations. State the two conditions under which resetting it is safe, and check the batch loop on the back.
back:
Answer: an arena reserves one large buffer and hands out aligned pieces by moving a pointer forward. Allocation is a few instructions and there is no per-object delete. reset() releases everything at once.

Resetting is safe only if (1) no pointer or reference into the arena is used after the reset, and (2) the objects stored in it are trivially destructible, since reset() runs no destructors. Non-trivial types need placement new and explicit destruction. A single arena is not thread-safe, so each worker thread needs its own.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <new>

class Arena {
public:
    explicit Arena(std::size_t bytes) : buf_(new std::byte[bytes]), cap_(bytes) {}
    void* allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t align) {
        std::size_t p = (used_ + align - 1) & ~(align - 1);   // align: power of two
        if (p + n > cap_) throw std::bad_alloc{};
        used_ = p + n;
        return buf_.get() + p;
    }
    void reset() noexcept { used_ = 0; }     // O(1): releases everything, runs no destructors
    std::size_t used() const noexcept { return used_; }
private:
    std::unique_ptr<std::byte[]> buf_;
    std::size_t cap_;
    std::size_t used_ = 0;
};

int main() {
    Arena arena(1 << 16);
    for (int batch = 0; batch < 3; ++batch) {
        const std::size_t n = 1000;
        double* paths = static_cast<double*>(arena.allocate(n * sizeof(double), alignof(double)));
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) paths[i] = static_cast<double>(i) * 0.5 + batch;
        std::printf("batch %d: used=%zu bytes, paths[999]=%.1f\n", batch, arena.used(), paths[999]);
        arena.reset();
    }
}
Output:
batch 0: used=8000 bytes, paths[999]=499.5
batch 1: used=8000 bytes, paths[999]=500.5
batch 2: used=8000 bytes, paths[999]=501.5
Interview trap: the alignment must be a power of two for the mask to work. In practice the arena is sized for the worst batch, and an overflow should be an error, not a silent reallocation that would invalidate every pointer already handed out.

front: Implement a minimal UniquePtr<T> that supports move and forbids copy. Which members must it have for an interview answer, and which edge case do candidates usually miss? Check the implementation and output on the back.
back:
Answer: the essential members are the explicit pointer constructor, a destructor that deletes, the deleted copy operations, the move constructor and move assignment, operator*, operator->, get, release, reset and an explicit operator bool. Move assignment needs the self-check and must delete the old pointer before taking the new one.

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

template <class T>
class UniquePtr {
public:
    explicit UniquePtr(T* p = nullptr) noexcept : p_(p) {}
    ~UniquePtr() { delete p_; }

    UniquePtr(const UniquePtr&) = delete;
    UniquePtr& operator=(const UniquePtr&) = delete;

    UniquePtr(UniquePtr&& o) noexcept : p_(std::exchange(o.p_, nullptr)) {}
    UniquePtr& operator=(UniquePtr&& o) noexcept {
        if (this != &o) {
            delete p_;
            p_ = std::exchange(o.p_, nullptr);
        }
        return *this;
    }

    T& operator*() const noexcept { return *p_; }
    T* operator->() const noexcept { return p_; }
    T* get() const noexcept { return p_; }
    T* release() noexcept { return std::exchange(p_, nullptr); }
    void reset(T* p = nullptr) noexcept { T* old = std::exchange(p_, p); delete old; }
    explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return p_ != nullptr; }

private:
    T* p_;
};

struct Position { int qty; };

int main() {
    UniquePtr<Position> a(new Position{10});
    UniquePtr<Position> b = std::move(a);
    std::printf("b->qty=%d a=%d\n", b->qty, static_cast<int>(static_cast<bool>(a)));
    b.reset(new Position{20});
    std::printf("after reset qty=%d\n", (*b).qty);
    Position* raw = b.release();
    std::printf("released qty=%d b=%d\n", raw->qty, static_cast<int>(static_cast<bool>(b)));
    delete raw;
}
Output:
b->qty=10 a=0
after reset qty=20
released qty=20 b=0
Interview trap: the constructor must be explicit. Without it, UniquePtr<T> p = new T; compiles, and any function taking a UniquePtr silently accepts a raw pointer, which creates an owner nobody expects. Also say what is not covered: array form, deleters and allocator support.
